author: Ben Feifke
text:
Everybody's going crazy about Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs)... but what if they're wrong?


💡 I was interviewing a candidate last week, and he said something that stuck with me:

"The forward deployed engineer will eventually just become a customer service role."


🤔 At first I pushed back. But then I thought about the "Lindy Effect", which says: 

"The expected remaining lifetime of non-perishable things (like technologies or books) is proportional to how long it's already existed."


So, a book that's been in print for 100 years will probably be in print for another 100; a job title that's been around for 3 months... may only last another 3 months.


📊 Consider:

- "Data Scientist" has been around since ~2008. Still here, but the definition keeps shifting, and it fell dramatically out of fashion compared to ML Engineer and Data Engineer

- "Analytics Engineer" was effectively created by dbt ~7 years ago. Already feeling the pressure from AI tooling?

- "Forward Deployed Engineer" became popular... late last year?


🔮 My take: FDEs are real and valuable today. But the role might evolve faster than people expect. After all, don't forget -- it's only 2-3 years ago that the market was going crazy hiring Prompt Engineers!

- The "forward deployed" part, delivering customer success, that's timeless.

- The "engineer" part, building elegant software solutions, that's also timeless.

- 💡 The hypothesis here is that the blend of the two might not be necessary for so long.


Maybe in 5 years, an "FDE" is really just a technical account manager with great prompting skills...

I don't know, time will tell...


What do you think: are FDEs really here to stay, or are they yet another transitional role in the tech job market? 👇

A US healthcare software company has just bought an agentic voice AI team built in Vilnius, and the part that interests me is where the engineers end up.

Povilas Gudzius, and Nikita Pajanok started Spike Technologies as a health data API in 2024, rebuilt it into genuinely agentic voice AI for revenue cycle work, and that reengineered capability is what Nick Hedges and Raintree Systems wanted to own. 

Terms were not disclosed, but the logic is clear: it is faster to acquire a proven applied-AI team than to build one.

What I keep telling hiring managers is that the Baltic exit map now has three routes, and the least discussed is being bought for the team. When that team stays in Vilnius, as it does here, the market keeps its scarce voice-AI and ML engineers and gains another operator who has taken a product from seed to exit. That is exactly the talent that seeds the next generation of Lithuanian AI companies.

If you are hiring applied-AI or ML engineers in the Baltics, you are competing with US acquirers now, not just the ever growing number of local scale-ups. 

Congratulations to all teams involved!

text:
AI is changing what strong technical teams look like.
Not by replacing people.
By changing what people need to be great at.
 
The tech industry is focusing in the same direction:
critical thinking, synthesis, verification, and interdisciplinary judgment are becoming more valuable.
 
That has real hiring implications.
 
If every candidate can use AI tools,
the differentiator is no longer access.
It is judgment.
 
What to screen for now:
 
1. Can they validate output?
Not just produce it.
 
2. Can they work across context?
Product, engineering, operations, compliance, customer needs.
 
3. Can they communicate tradeoffs clearly?
Especially in remote talent environments.
 
4. Can they improve workflows?
Not just complete tickets.
 
A practical interview prompt:
Give a candidate an AI-generated technical solution with two hidden flaws.
Then ask:
What would you trust?
What would you verify?
What would you change before shipping?
 
That reveals far more than asking whether they have used AI/ML tools.
 
As the market stays selective and engineering roles evolve, the best talent acquisition process will likely favor people who pair technical depth with strong judgment.
 
That is especially true for scaling tech teams where one hire can shape delivery quality for months.

---

모델을 잘 만드는 것만으로는 예전만큼 차별화가 되지 않는 것 같습니다.

JD 키워드가 조금씩 바뀌고 있습니다. 'ML Engineer'에서 'DS + Business Impact'로. 매출, CAC, LTV를 직접 움직인 경험을 보는 흐름입니다. 모델링 실력은 기본값에 가까워지고 있고, 그게 비즈니스 숫자로 어떻게 연결됐는지를 함께 보는 경우가 많아졌습니다.

-

Causal Inference가 시니어 DS의 문턱이 되고 있는 것 같습니다.

A/B 설계와 인과 추론 경험 유무가 서류에서 걸러지는 경우가 늘고 있습니다. 흥미로운 건 이 역량을 실전에서 써본 분이 생각보다 많지 않다는 점입니다. 알고는 있는데 직접 설계해본 경험이 있는 분이 드문 것 같습니다.

-

커머스·광고 도메인 DS가 오히려 귀해진 것 같습니다.

LLM 붐 이후 실전 커머스 경험자들이 AI 쪽으로 이동하면서 역설적으로 풀이 얇아진 느낌입니다. 서치를 하다보면 예전만큼 후보자가 많지 않습니다. 이 도메인에 계신 분들의 협상력이 오히려 올라가 있는 시점인 것 같습니다.

-

배포까지 해봤냐가 기술 면접에서 자주 나오는 질문이 됐습니다.

MLOps 경험 없이 시니어 포지션을 통과하기가 쉽지 않은 흐름입니다. 모델을 만들 수 있는 분은 많은데 프로덕션까지 가져가 본 분은 생각보다 적다는 게 기업 HR팀과 CTO 조직에서 자주 나오는 이야기입니다.

-

포지션 공고는 DS인데 실제로는 MLE에 가까운 경우가 많습니다.

요즘 DS 포지션 JD를 열어보면 Feature Store, MLflow, Airflow가 기본으로 들어가 있는 경우가 꽤 있습니다. 이 경계를 넘나들 수 있는 분들에게는 오히려 기회가 되는 시점인 것 같습니다.

----

Please apply only if media excites you.

This industry is demanding. It moves every hour. You have to care about stories, creators, news, sports, entertainment, culture, and technology. The people who thrive here aren't just technically brilliant, they're endlessly curious.

We're looking for intent. Curiosity. Ownership. And people who want to stand out by building things that matter.
